item.title: Votualevu residents without water since Saturday night as WAF works to restore supply
item.description: Some residents of Votualevu, Nadi, have been without water since Saturday night, with concerns growing over the prolonged disruption. Savalau Road resident Raju Singh Desi says water cuts have occurred intermittently in his area, but the latest disruption has lasted longer than usual.
item.content:encoded:
Some residents of Votualevu, Nadi, have been without water since Saturday night, with concerns growing over the prolonged disruption.

Savalau Road resident Raju Singh Desi says water cuts have occurred intermittently in his area, but the latest disruption has lasted longer than usual.

Desi says the situation is unusual, as residents have not experienced a water cut lasting this long before.

The Water Authority of Fiji says it has been gradually restoring the system since this morning and will continue work tonight.

WAF says it is filling the pipes and flushing the pipeline properly to prevent air voids, which could result in further burst mains.

Residents are waiting for water supply to be fully restored.

item.title: Sayed-Khaiyum raises concerns over social pension cuts, Kiran clarifies eligibility
item.description: Senior citizens who own basic household items such as a TV and a refrigerator are not automatically disqualified from receiving social pensions. This has been clarified by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran following comments made by former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum that some older people had reportedly stopped receiving their pensions after being subjected
item.content:encoded:
Senior citizens who own basic household items such as a TV and a refrigerator are not automatically disqualified from receiving social pensions.

This has been clarified by Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran following comments made by former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum that some older people had reportedly stopped receiving their pensions after being subjected to asset tests.

In a recent interview, Sayed-Khaiyum said many people who used to receive social pensions were no longer receiving them.

He said many people in Fiji work as domestic helpers, roadside sellers and farmers, particularly in villages, but do not have access to the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) because they have never worked in formal employment.

Sayed-Khaiyum said these people often have no retirement savings to rely on when they grow old.

He said the Social Pension Scheme initially provided $50 a month to people aged 70 and above who had never been members of the FNPF, before being expanded to cover those aged 65 and above, with payments increased to $100 a month.

Sayed-Khaiyum said he had been told that some older people in Lautoka were no longer receiving the assistance, despite previously being eligible.

He said some had reportedly undergone asset tests.

He added that because they own assets such as refrigetrators and television, they no longer get pension money.

In response, Kiran says the statements appear to confuse the Social Pension Scheme with the Family Assistance Scheme, which are separate programmes with different objectives, assessment processes and eligibility criteria.

She says eligible Fiji citizens aged 65 and above who do not receive an FNPF pension or another qualifying superannuation benefit may qualify for the Social Pension Scheme, subject to its eligibility requirements.

She says the scheme supported 51,784 senior citizens in 2023, with a budget of $57.4 million and 96 per cent budget utilisation.

For the 2025–2026 financial year, the Government increased the allocation to $82.06 million, supporting 59,918 recipients.

This represents an increase of 8,134 recipients, or 15.7 per cent, compared with 2023, alongside an additional $24.66 million in budget allocation.

Kiran says supporting vulnerable older persons, including former informal workers, subsistence farmers and market vendors with limited retirement savings, remains a priority.

She says more than 130,000 beneficiaries currently receive assistance through six major social welfare programmes.

It is also implementing reforms to improve transparency, accountability and service delivery, including reviewing social assistance programmes, improving poverty-targeting methods and strengthening verification processes.

She says anyone who believes their assistance has been stopped incorrectly should use its established grievance and review processes so their individual circumstances can be assessed.

She says eligibility decisions must follow the correct programme rules while ensuring public funds are administered responsibly.

item.title: Calls for urgent attention to HIV prevention and treatment in correctional facilities
item.description: Questions have been raised over whether people held in correctional facilities are included in the needle-syringe programme aimed at preventing HIV transmission. This was raised by Opposition MP Mareca Baba during 2026 Fiji Women's Practice Parliament saying 18 people tested positive for HIV upon admission to one correctional facility during a 60-day period between April and May this year.
item.content:encoded:
Questions have been raised over whether people held in correctional facilities are included in the needle-syringe programme aimed at preventing HIV transmission.

This was raised by Opposition MP Mareca Baba during 2026 Fiji Women's Practice Parliament saying 18 people tested positive for HIV upon admission to one correctional facility during a 60-day period between April and May this year.

Baba says that between April and May this year, 42 Fijians were admitted to one correctional facility over a period of 60 days.

Of these, 32 were under the age of 40, five were under 50, two were between 51 and 65, and two were just 19 years old.

Baba adds 36 of the 42 people received prison sentences of less than 12 months.

She says people in custody must have access to HIV testing, support and treatment, as they eventually return to their communities.

Baba is calling on the Government to provide more funding for healthcare, rehabilitation and treatment services inside correctional facilities.

Baba is also calling for improved prison conditions and reduced overcrowding, saying minor offenders who do not pose a danger to the community should be diverted into treatment programmes instead of being sent to prison.

She says bail and remand practices should also be reviewed to ensure people are not held on remand longer than necessary.

Baba says a national HIV response must include people in prison and cannot stop at the gates of correctional facilities.

item.title: Fiji and US join forces to protect families and farmers from disease threats
item.description: Fijian families and farmers could be better protected from infectious diseases and threats to agricultural production, through a new partnership between Fiji and the United States aimed at detecting diseases earlier and responding before outbreaks spread further. The Strengthening Infectious Disease Detection Systems (STRIDES) programme was launched at Tamavua Twomey Hospital this afternoon , brin
item.content:encoded:
Fijian families and farmers could be better protected from infectious diseases and threats to agricultural production, through a new partnership between Fiji and the United States aimed at detecting diseases earlier and responding before outbreaks spread further.

The Strengthening Infectious Disease Detection Systems (STRIDES) programme was launched at Tamavua Twomey Hospital this afternoon , bringing together the Ministry of Health and Medical Services, the Ministry of Agriculture and Waterways, the United States Government and other partners.

Speaking at the launch, Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Health Dr Aalisha Sahu Khan says Fiji's experiences with COVID-19, dengue and influenza have shown the importance of having strong health systems in place before an outbreak occurs.

Dr Sahu Khan says Fiji already has capable laboratories and dedicated health workers, but ensuring these services remain reliable and effective in the long term is important.

She says the programme will help improve laboratory facilities, maintain reliable supplies, strengthen the skills of health workers and allow faster sharing of test results so authorities can respond quickly to disease threats.

Dr Sahu Khan also highlights the importance of stronger cooperation between human and animal health services, along with regular emergency response exercises to ensure Fiji is prepared for future outbreaks.

Meanwhile, Minister for Agriculture and Waterways Tomasi Tunabuna says the programme is equally important for protecting farmers, livestock and food security.

Tunabuna says thousands of families depend on healthy crops, livestock and reliable agricultural production for their livelihoods.

He says climate change is already affecting Fiji's food production through changing rainfall patterns, prolonged dry periods, severe flooding, rising temperatures and increasing risks from pests and diseases.

The Minister says these challenges threaten food security, livelihoods and the country's long-term development.

Tunabuna says the health of people, animals and the environment is closely connected, and a disease outbreak affecting one can have consequences for the others.

He says stronger disease monitoring, laboratory testing and biosecurity measures will help Fiji identify threats earlier, reduce losses for farmers and protect agricultural production.

Tunabuna adds that improving biosecurity will also help protect food supplies and strengthen confidence among farmers and investors.

Meanwhile, United States Chargé d’Affaires Christina Cavallo says the partnership will help Fiji identify infectious disease threats sooner, respond faster and save lives.

Cavallo says the United States will support improvements in laboratory testing for humans and animals, the safe transport of samples and stronger laboratory safety measures.

She says training will also be provided for laboratory workers and disease monitoring staff, while information sharing between agencies will be strengthened.

The US Embassy says the programme was developed in consultation with Fiji's health and agriculture leaders, laboratory scientists, disease monitoring teams and biosecurity officials.

It says the initiative will also help protect people across the Pacific by reducing the risk of infectious diseases spreading between countries.

STRIDES is led by international development organisation FHI 360, together with its partners Black & Veatch and PATH.

The programme aims to strengthen Fiji's preparedness for future disease outbreaks while protecting public health, agricultural production and livelihoods.
